**Design matrix: intercept and linear term**

Read one row as b₀ + b₁xᵢ. For all five inputs, the equations stack into Xb. The first column is x⁰ = 1, including the intercept entry at x = 0. The second column is x itself. The design and its curve appear together in [[ref:ex:l8-basis-linear-script]].

**Design matrix: intercept and squared term**

Keep the constant column and square every input in the second column. This column multiplies b₂. There is no b₁ term. The parabola has its vertex at x = 0; only its right side is shown. The design and its curve appear together in [[ref:ex:l8-basis-square-script]].

**Design matrix: intercept, x and x²**

Keep both transformed columns. The x term tilts the parabola and shifts its vertex. Higher powers x³ and x⁴ are further columns if the model calls for them. The design and its curve appear together in [[ref:ex:l8-basis-quadratic-script]].

**Design matrix: combine sinh and cosh**

Use dimensionless x. The sinh column changes sign across zero, while cosh has the same value at x and minus x. Their weights are independent. These are hyperbolic functions; a reciprocal term is a different way to obtain a hyperbola. The design and its curve appear together in [[ref:ex:l8-basis-hyperbolic-script]].

**Design matrix: exponential column**

Exponentiate each dimensionless input before fitting. The multiplier of exp(x) is a coefficient. If an unknown coefficient were placed inside the exponential, the model would no longer be linear in that coefficient. The design and its curve appear together in [[ref:ex:l8-basis-exp-script]].

**Design matrix: logarithmic column**

Use positive, dimensionless inputs. The logarithm acts on x, while the response remains on its original scale. This differs from fitting a logarithm of the measured response. The design and its curve appear together in [[ref:ex:l8-basis-log-script]].

**Design matrix: reciprocal column**

Use nonzero x. Here the five inputs are positive and the curve tends toward the intercept. The reciprocal is undefined at zero, so never draw a continuous curve through zero. The design and its curve appear together in [[ref:ex:l8-basis-reciprocal-script]].

**Design matrix: square-root column**

For real-valued square roots, x must be nonnegative. This case uses the same five positive inputs as the exponential, logarithm and reciprocal examples. The transform is fixed before fitting. The design and its curve appear together in [[ref:ex:l8-basis-sqrt-script]].

**Design matrix: mix several functions**

The first five rows and a curve for chosen weights appear in [[ref:ex:l8-basis-mixed-script]]. The coefficient vector is (4, −0.15, 1.5, −1.2, 1.1, −2, 0.9) in the same order as the columns. Each additional fixed function comes with its own weight. The five displayed rows alone cannot identify all seven weights.

**How many columns can we fit?**

Read [[ref:ex:l8-basis-column-limit-script]] with \(p\) counting all estimated coefficients, including the intercept. A unique ordinary least-squares solution requires independent columns, which implies \(p\leq n\). With \(p=n\) and full rank, the fit interpolates the data and leaves zero residual degrees of freedom. If we want at least one residual degree of freedom, use \(p\leq n-1\). This count is necessary; we still need to check column independence.

**Design matrix: eight rows for seven coefficients**

In [[ref:ex:l8-basis-eight-rows-script]], add three input rows at 1.5, 2.5 and 3.5 to the five-row design. At full precision, the seven columns are independent. Given eight observed responses, the coefficient fit is unique and the residual degrees of freedom are \(8-7=1\). The curve uses the same chosen weights as the previous illustration.

**When is a model linear in its coefficients?**

The comparisons in [[ref:ex:l8-fixed-basis-coefficients-script]] use the same design-matrix rule: a term of the form \(b_j f_j(x)\) contributes the fixed column \(f_j(x)\). In \(\sinh(xb_4)\) and \(\exp(xb_2)\), the unknown changes the column itself, so fitting the original coefficient requires nonlinear regression. In \(\exp(x+b_2)\), factor out \(\exp(b_2)\) and fit \(u\) as the new linear coefficient multiplying the known column \(\exp(x)\). A real \(b_2=\ln(u)\) can only be recovered for \(u>0\). If an unconstrained fit gives \(u\leq 0\), it does not correspond to the original model.

**Five inputs, three design columns**

The matrix and model curve appear together in [[ref:ex:l8-gram-design-script]]. Use the five input values 1, 4, 9, 16 and 25. The columns are the constant one, x itself and the square root of x. The plotted curve is Xb at those inputs and the same model evaluated between them, using chosen coefficients.

**From one squared length to XᵀX**

Apply the column-product rule from [[ref:ex:l8-column-squares-script]] to each pair in [[ref:ex:l8-gram-rule-script]]. Recall that e transpose e is one dot product of a column with itself. X transpose X applies that rule to every pair of columns. A diagonal entry sums squares of one column. An off-diagonal entry sums products of two different columns in matching rows.

**Calculate XᵀX for the five inputs**

Use the design and curve in [[ref:ex:l8-gram-design-script]] as context for the matrix calculation in [[ref:ex:l8-gram-worked-script]]. Read the second column as x and the third as square roots. Multiply matching entries and sum. To get the second diagonal entry, square every x and add. To get entry row two, column three, multiply x by its square root in each row and add. Its mirror entry has the same value. Repeat with the column of ones and the third column to complete the matrix.

**Calculate Xᵀy from the measured responses**

In [[ref:ex:l8-xty-worked-script]], use the same design as in [[ref:ex:l8-gram-design-script]] and add a column of measured responses. Keep the same five input rows and align the example measurements 2, 3, 5, 6 and 9 with them in order. Multiply each design column entry by the matching measured response and add the five products. The constant column gives the response sum, the x column gives 380, and the square-root column gives 92. This is the right-hand side of the normal equation.

**The coefficient formula: what is still missing?**

See [[ref:ex:l8-inverse-remaining-script]]. We already have both products. Call X transpose X G and X transpose y r. The inverse notation describes the solution. We can get the same coefficients by solving G beta hat equals r directly. Refer back to [[ref:ex:l8-gram-worked-script]] for \(X^\top X\) and [[ref:ex:l8-xty-worked-script]] for \(X^\top y\). If the columns of \(X\) are independent, \(G\) is invertible and the formula may also be written as \(\widehat\beta=G^{-1}X^\top y\).

**Two ways to handle the inverse**

For an invertible two-by-two matrix, use the determinant formula. For a symmetric positive-definite matrix, use Cholesky factorisation. Cholesky factors can be used to form the inverse or solve the normal equations directly. Use the references to read more about each method. See the comparison in [[ref:ex:l8-inverse-methods-script]]. Further reading: [[ref:ex:l8-inverse-methods-determinant-script]] and [[ref:ex:l8-inverse-methods-cholesky-script]].
entities.label: Design matrices and cross-products

entities.description:
**Build the drift design and response**

Starting from the five readings in [[ref:ex:l8-script-material-1-1]], [[ref:ex:l8-drift-products-script]] lists the rows of \(X\) and \(y\) together. Pair the intercept column with itself to count five observations. Its product with the time column is \(0+1+2+3+4=10\), and the time column with itself gives \(0^2+1^2+2^2+3^2+4^2=30\). These fill \(X^\top X\). For \(X^\top y\), the intercept pairs with the readings to give their sum, 25 mV. The time column weights those readings by 0 through 4 min, giving 69.9 min·mV.

**Back to the detector: fit the drift line**

Substitute the products from [[ref:ex:l8-drift-products-script]] in [[ref:ex:l8-drift-fit-script]]. The determinant is \(5\cdot30-10^2=50\). Multiplying the inverse by \(X^\top y\) gives an intercept of 1.02 mV and a slope of 1.99 mV/min.

**Back to the detector: predict the signal at 2.5 min**

Return to the five detector readings from [[ref:ex:l8-script-material-1-1]]. The least-squares line shown in [[ref:ex:l8-drift-prediction-script]] is \(\widehat y=1.02+1.99t\), with \(t\) in minutes and \(\widehat y\) in millivolts. Evaluating it at 2.5 min gives \(1.02+1.99\cdot2.5=5.995\) mV. The requested time falls between two observed times, so this is interpolation.

**A heating ramp with a changing rate**

The temperature was recorded once a minute for four minutes. The least-squares straight line in [[ref:ex:l8-heating-straight-check-script]] assumes a constant change per minute. Its residuals are positive at both ends and negative in the middle. That systematic pattern suggests that the temperature rises faster later in the run.

**Add a column for squared time**

In [[ref:ex:l8-heating-quadratic-fit-script]], each row pairs one observation with three known inputs. The intercept column contains ones. The next column contains elapsed time \(x\) in minutes, and the third contains its square \(x^2\) in minutes squared. At 3 min, for example, the inputs are 1, 3 and 9, and the observed response is 29.66 °C. The same ordinary least-squares procedure estimates three coefficients. The fitted coefficients are 21.00 °C for the intercept, 0.50 °C/min for time and 0.80 °C/min² for squared time. The sum of squared residuals falls from 8.964 °C² for the line to 0.004 °C² for the quadratic fit on these observations.

**An exponential decay on two scales**

[[ref:ex:l8-log-decay-observations-script]] starts with five tracer concentrations in mg/L. The first one-minute drop is about 5.65 mg/L, while the last is only about 1.67 mg/L. If a similar fraction of the tracer remains after each minute, the same relative loss translates into a smaller absolute drop as the concentration declines.

The transformation in [[ref:ex:l8-log-decay-transform-script]] divides each positive measured concentration by the reference of 1 mg/L before taking its natural logarithm. Time stays in minutes. The difference between two consecutive logarithms is the logarithm of the ratio of their concentrations. A constant retention fraction therefore produces an equal step for each equal time interval.

In [[ref:ex:l8-log-decay-fit-script]], both panels show the same observations. The line in [[ref:ex:l8-log-decay-line-formula-script]] is fitted by ordinary least squares on the log scale, with an intercept of about 2.996 and a slope of −0.40 per minute. Apply the exponential in the second equation to the fitted log values to recover a curve in mg/L. Each minute the model retains about 67% of the preceding concentration. The regression minimises squared errors on the log scale.

**Multiple linear regression with two measured predictors**

[[ref:ex:l8-multiple-regression-design-script]] shows six synthetic detector readings for three concentrations at two temperatures. Each row pairs both settings with one response. The design columns contain ones, the measured concentration, and the measured temperature in °C. As in earlier examples, ordinary least squares estimates all coefficients at once.

[[ref:ex:l8-multiple-regression-products-script]] starts from the same six rows. Apply [[ref:ex:l8-multiple-regression-products-formula-script]] by multiplying entries in corresponding rows and adding the products. For example, pairing concentration with temperature gives \((20+30)(1+2+3)=300\). This value appears in both symmetric positions of \(X^\top X\). For \(X^\top y\), the ones sum the six signals to 33, the concentrations weight them to give 74, and the measured temperatures weight them to give 840.

In [[ref:ex:l8-multiple-regression-coefficients-script]], substitute the two products in the coefficient formula. Multiplying by the inverse yields −1.00 mV for the intercept, 2.00 mV per mg/L for the concentration slope, and 0.10 mV per °C for the temperature slope. The intercept is the model prediction at zero concentration and 0 °C, outside the measured settings.

In [[ref:ex:l8-multiple-regression-plane-script]], the fitted signal forms a plane above the two predictor axes. Fixing temperature at 20 or 30 °C cuts that plane along a straight line. Both cuts have the same concentration slope because the model uses a single concentration coefficient. The six dots are the measured signals at the corresponding concentration and temperature.

[[ref:ex:l8-multiple-regression-fit-script]] plots the fitted signal against concentration at two fixed temperatures. The coefficient of concentration measures the change in fitted signal per mg/L while temperature stays fixed. The temperature coefficient measures the change per degree while concentration stays fixed. In [[ref:ex:l8-multiple-regression-fit-formula-script]], this works out to 2 mV per mg/L and 1 mV per 10 °C. The fitted profiles are parallel because the model assigns a common concentration slope to both temperatures. The next example uses the same regression with 0/1 predictors for a categorical variable.
entities.label: From the formula to fitted models

entities.description:
**One-way ANOVA as a linear regression**

The river-water SPE example from Level 7 has eighteen independent preparations, six per method. In [[ref:ex:l8-anova-recovery-design-script]], the response column contains the original recoveries. The design matrix has a column of ones and two 0/1 indicators, for methods B and C. Method A is the reference because both indicators are zero for its rows. An additional indicator for A would make the columns dependent, since the three indicators sum to the intercept column.

In [[ref:ex:l8-anova-recovery-products-script]], the design rows are grouped by method and each pattern occurs six times. The products in [[ref:ex:l8-anova-recovery-products-formula-script]] show why the intercept counts 18, B and C each count six, and their overlap is zero. Multiplying by the observed responses sums 1710 across all preparations and selects the method totals 588 for B and 558 for C.

[[ref:ex:l8-anova-recovery-coefficients-script]] applies the inverse to those sums. Its first row takes the total minus the B and C sums, leaving 564 for method A. Dividing by six gives 94% recovery. The other two rows give the differences from A, +4 and −1 percentage points.

[[ref:ex:l8-anova-recovery-fit-script]] compares two ordinary least-squares models. The intercept-only model predicts the grand mean (95%) for every sample. The model with method predicts the mean of each group (94%, 98%, 93%). With A as the reference, the fitted intercept is 94% and the two adjustments are +4 and −1 percentage points. The null hypothesis of equal group means is the joint hypothesis that both adjustments are zero.

In [[ref:ex:l8-anova-recovery-formula-script]], the drop in residual sum of squares from 114 to 30 is the between-method sum of squares, 84. The group model adds two coefficients and leaves fifteen residual degrees of freedom. Substitution in [[ref:ex:l8-anova-recovery-formula-script]] gives \(F=(84/2)/(30/15)=21\), the same statistic as one-way ANOVA. This comparison uses the classical ANOVA assumptions when interpreting the F test.

entities.description:
**Linear Regression**

Today we turn a time trend into a reproducible fitted model. We first agree what a good line means, then acquire enough matrix language to build a design matrix and derive the normal equations. The final applications change the known model terms without changing the linear coefficient problem. Uncertainty belongs to the next appointment.
**A signal drifts during a run**

During one run, we recorded the detector signal at the start and then once per minute. The figure pairs the detector setup with the five readings: 1.10, 2.80, 5.20, 6.90 and 9.00 mV at 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 min, respectively. How can we predict the signal at 2.5 min, between two recorded times? A model describes signal as a function of time. We can evaluate it inside the measured interval (interpolation) or outside it (extrapolation). The dashed extension in the figure is an extrapolation beyond the last reading. Adding a model raises the next question: how do we choose a line that fits the measured points?

[[ref:ex:l8-script-material-1-1]]

**Estimate a model from measurements**

To describe the measured trend with a straight line, we estimate two numbers using all five time–signal pairs. The intercept gives the modelled signal at zero minutes in mV. The slope gives the modelled change in signal per minute in mV/min. The schematic shows how the measurements inform both coefficients. In the interactive plot, you can change each one and see what happens to the line.

[[ref:ex:l8-script-material-estimate-line]]

**Fit by eye: two coefficients**

Try different candidate lines for the same measurements. Change the intercept to raise or lower the line; change the slope to alter its tilt in mV per minute. The manual experiment starts at intercept 0 mV and slope 2.5 mV/min. As you move the sliders, compare the vertical gaps in the scatter plot with the residual bars. A point above the line appears above zero in the residual plot, and a point below the line appears below zero. Ask learners to improve the line and explain which vertical gaps their changes reduce. Do not reveal the fitted coefficient values yet. Compare the visible candidate curve with the fixed observation points; later the normal equations provide a reproducible solution.

[[ref:ex:l8-script-material-1-2]]

[[ref:ex:l8-script-material-1-3]]

**Give every vertical gap a sign**

Use the adjustable candidate line in [[ref:ex:l8-script-material-1-2]] to connect the scatter plot with the residual bars. Compute each observation minus its prediction at exactly the same time. A point above the line has positive residual; one below has negative residual. Move the sliders and check how the signed residuals change. These are vertical signal gaps, not perpendicular geometric distances.

**What happens when we add the signed gaps?**

Adding the five residuals gives 0.00 mV. Each point still misses the fitted line: positive and negative gaps cancel. The next step is to define a score that counts gaps on both sides.
**What should we minimise to fit a line?**

The comparison figure uses the same five measurements for two candidate lines. The starting line has intercept 0 mV and slope 2.5 mV/min, with residuals +1.10, +0.30, +0.20, −0.60 and −1.00 mV. The other line has intercept 1 mV and slope 2 mV/min, with residuals +0.10, −0.20, +0.20, −0.10 and 0.00 mV. Both signed sums are zero. Squaring the residuals before adding gives 2.70 mV² for the first line and 0.10 mV² for the second. A gap twice as large contributes four times as much. Absolute deviations would also prevent cancellation. The squared score is differentiable in the coefficients, which is useful when we derive the normal equations.

[[ref:ex:l8-script-material-1-7]]

[[ref:ex:l8-script-material-1-8]]

**Where is the squared error smallest?**

With the observations fixed, try changing one coefficient at a time. Each local error plot shows a slice of the squared-error surface near the corresponding slider setting. The other coefficient is held at its current value. Both plots mark the same current squared error. The total differential gives the first-order change in squared error for a change in both coefficients. At the joint minimum it is zero for every direction. We can vary one coefficient while keeping the other fixed. Doing this for each coefficient shows that both partial derivatives must be zero at the same pair of values. For these data, the quadratic curves upward and the pair is unique. To find the pair we need to solve the two equations together. Matrix notation gives us a compact way to do that.

[[ref:ex:l8-minimum-two-coefficients-script-1]]

[[ref:ex:l8-minimum-two-coefficients-script-2]]

**Matrix Algebra**

This short detour introduces the operations we will use to express the two regression conditions together.

**Matrix Shapes: count rows before columns**

Compare the 2 by 3, 3 by 2 and 2 by 4 arrays. Count horizontal rows first and vertical columns second. The first two arrays contain the same number of entries, but their shapes differ.

[[ref:ex:l8-script-material-2-2]]

**Matrix Indexing: row first, then column**

Read a subscript pair in a fixed order. In the shown matrix, a subscript 23 means row 2 then column 3, so its value is 6. It does not mean row 3 column 2, and it does not mean the number twenty-three. The box marks that matrix entry.

[[ref:ex:l8-script-material-2-4]]

**Matrix Types: square matrices**

Compare the 2 by 2, 3 by 3 and 4 by 4 examples. Every one is square because its row and column counts match. The positions and values of the entries can vary.

[[ref:ex:l8-script-material-2-6]]

**Matrix Types: diagonal matrices**

Compare diagonal matrices of sizes 2, 3 and 4. The highlighted diagonal is where the row and column indices agree. Every off-diagonal entry is zero. The 3 by 3 example has a zero on its main diagonal, which makes it singular.

[[ref:ex:l8-script-material-2-7]]

**Matrix Types: identity matrices**

Compare the identities of sizes 1, 2 and 3. Every diagonal entry is one. The left identity for a 2 by 3 matrix must have size 2, and the right identity must have size 3. Both products preserve the same matrix A.

[[ref:ex:l8-script-material-2-8]]

**Matrix Arithmetic: addition and subtraction**

Both matrices have the same shape. Read the top-left cells first: add 1 and 5 or subtract 5 from 1. Then do the same at each of the other three positions. The result keeps the original shape. When entries have units, the two values being combined must have compatible units.

[[ref:ex:l8-script-material-2-9]]

**Matrix Arithmetic: multiplication by a scalar**

Multiply each entry by the same scalar. The first calculation multiplies 1 by 2, and the remaining cells repeat the same operation with 2, 3 and 4. The positions and the shape stay the same. A dimensionless scalar preserves the units of the entries.

[[ref:ex:l8-script-material-2-10]]

**Matrix Transpose: rows become columns**

The first row [1,2,3] becomes the first column and the second row [4,5,6] becomes the second column. Shape two-by-three therefore becomes three-by-two. Transposing twice returns the original matrix. Later X transpose will collect dot products with the columns of X.

[[ref:ex:l8-script-material-2-11]]

**Matrix Multiplication: which dimensions must match?**

A matrix with m rows and n columns can multiply one with n rows and p columns. Each output entry needs a complete row and a complete column of equal length. The result has m rows and p columns. As a quick question, a two-by-three times a three-by-four is valid and yields two-by-four; the reverse order is not valid. Pause for the shape answer before continuing.

[[ref:ex:l8-script-material-2-12]]

**Matrix Multiplication: one row meets one column**

Each row of A has three entries and each column of B has three entries. Start with the boxed row and column. Multiply the three matching pairs and add to get 5 in the top-left cell. The other three cells use the three remaining row-column pairs and give 13, 14 and 31. The result has two rows from A and two columns from B.

[[ref:ex:l8-script-material-2-14]]

**Matrix Multiplication: sum the squares of a column**

Transpose the n by 1 column so that it becomes one row. Multiplying that row by the original column pairs each entry with itself and adds the products. For entries 2, 3 and 4 the result is 4 plus 9 plus 16, which is 29.

[[ref:ex:l8-column-squares-script]]

**Matrix Multiplication: why order matters**

Use a new pair of two-by-two matrices so both products have the same dimensions. The order still matters: AB and BA have different entries. Noncommutativity is about the operation, not a rounding error. For rectangular matrices one order may not even exist. Do not rearrange matrix factors as though they were scalar numbers.

[[ref:ex:l8-script-material-2-16]]

**Matrix Transpose: three useful rules**

Subtraction is entrywise, so swapping rows and columns preserves the difference between matching entries. For a product, the row of A and column of B become a column of A transpose and a row of B transpose. Their dot product is preserved by reversing the factors. Transposing a second time swaps the rows and columns back.

[[ref:ex:l8-transpose-rules-script]]

**Matrix Arithmetic: entrywise multiplication**

Hadamard multiplication combines corresponding entries of equally shaped matrices. For the same A and B it gives rows [5,12] and [21,32]. This is neither AB nor BA. In R, an asterisk is entrywise multiplication and percent-star-percent is matrix multiplication. Keep that distinction when reading model code.

[[ref:ex:l8-script-material-2-17]]

**Matrix Inverse: undoing a matrix product**

For the new example A = [[2,1],[1,1]], the inverse is [[1,−1],[−1,2]]. Check either multiplication order: the diagonal products sum to one and off-diagonal products sum to zero. An inverse is not obtained by taking reciprocals of individual entries. The inverse exists only for nonsingular square matrices.

[[ref:ex:l8-script-material-2-19]]

**Matrix Equations: write two equations as one**

The equations 2u1 + u2 = 5 and u1 + u2 = 3 become Au = b with the same inverse example and b = [5,3]. Left-multiply by the inverse to obtain u = [2,1]. Substitute back: 2 times 2 plus 1 equals 5 and 2 plus 1 equals 3. Row equations and the matrix equation describe the same problem.

[[ref:ex:l8-script-material-2-22]]

**Evaluate a line at five points**

Use the known intercept 2 and slope 0.5. Read the times in the order shown on the slide. Work through the first input 10, then build the whole matrix. The first column of ones carries the intercept into every row and the second column contains the five inputs. Each row times the same coefficient column yields one calculated response. Finally name the three objects X, b and y.

[[ref:ex:l8-five-point-matrix-script]]

**Back to the Least-Squares Minimum**

Return from matrix algebra to the five detector readings. We can now use matrix operations to find the coefficients that minimise the squared error.

**Recall the total differential**

In [[ref:ex:l8-minimum-two-coefficients-script-2]], \(Q\) is the squared error and \(\mathrm dQ\) describes its first-order change as the coefficients vary. At the minimum, \(\mathrm dQ\) vanishes in every coefficient direction. Start with the term inside the square brackets, the residual of one observation.

**Put the residuals into a column**

The five-point example [[ref:ex:l8-five-point-matrix-script]] shows how a row of the design matrix times the coefficient column gives one prediction. Here \(\beta\) denotes that same coefficient column. In [[ref:ex:l8-script-material-4-2]], subtract the predicted column \(X\beta\) from the observed column \(y\). This gives the residual column \(e\).

**Write squared error as a matrix product**

Apply the squared-column rule in [[ref:ex:l8-column-squares-script]] to the residual column. In [[ref:ex:l8-script-material-4-5]], replace both copies of \(e\) by \(y-X\beta\). The transpose rules in [[ref:ex:l8-transpose-rules-script]] preserve the minus sign and reverse the factors in \((X\beta)^\top\).

**Expand the squared error**

Distribute the brackets of [[ref:ex:l8-script-material-4-5]] to get the four products in [[ref:ex:l8-expand-squared-error-script]]. Keep the order of the factors. Apply the product transpose rule in [[ref:ex:l8-transpose-rules-script]] to \(y^\top X\beta\). Reversing the factors gives \(\beta^\top X^\top y\). The whole product is a scalar, so its transpose is equal to its original value. This is why the two mixed terms combine in the final line.

**Differentiate term by term**

In [[ref:ex:l8-script-material-4-6]], differentiate the expanded squared error in [[ref:ex:l8-expand-squared-error-script]] while keeping \(X\) and \(y\) fixed. The constant contributes zero. The mixed term contributes a fixed vector.

**Differentiate the quadratic term**

In [[ref:ex:l8-quadratic-gradient-script]], the product rule differentiates each of the two occurrences of \(\beta\) once. Because \(X^\top X\) is symmetric, the two resulting vector contributions are identical. Their sum is \(2X^\top X\beta\).

**Solve the normal equation**

Set the gradient from [[ref:ex:l8-quadratic-gradient-script]] to zero. In [[ref:ex:l8-script-material-2-23]], divide by two and move \(X^\top y\) to the right.

**Isolate the coefficients**

In [[ref:ex:l8-isolate-coefficients-script]], multiply both sides from the left by \((X^\top X)^{-1}\), which exists when the design columns are independent. On the left, the adjacent factors are the inverse followed by its matrix. Their product is the identity, and \(I\widehat\beta=\widehat\beta\).

**The coefficient formula**

The result in [[ref:ex:l8-main-ols-formula-script]] gives the fitted coefficients from \(X\) and \(y\). To use it, first choose the columns of \(X\).

scenes.narration: Today we turn a time trend into a reproducible fitted model. We first agree what a good line means, then acquire enough matrix language to build a design matrix and derive the normal equations. The final applications change the known model terms without changing the linear coefficient problem. Uncertainty belongs to the next appointment.

How can we predict the signal at 2.5 min?

scenes.narration: During one run, we recorded the detector signal at the start and then once per minute. Reveal the five readings, then mark 2.5 min between two observed times. blocks.text: Squaring prevents cancellation and gives larger misses more weight.

scenes.narration: Compare two lines against the same five measurements. Ask which would get the smaller score by adding residuals as they are. Both sums are zero because the positive and negative gaps cancel. Reveal the squared sums: 2.70 for the line we started with and 0.10 for the closer candidate. Squaring prevents cancellation and makes a gap twice as large count four times as much. Choose coefficients that minimise this total. Absolute gaps also avoid cancellation. The squared score is smooth in the coefficients, which will let us derive equations for the minimum.

sections.body:
**Linear Regression**

Today we turn a time trend into a reproducible fitted model. We first agree what a good line means, then acquire enough matrix language to build a design matrix and derive the normal equations. The final applications change the known model terms without changing the linear coefficient problem. Uncertainty belongs to the next appointment.
**A signal drifts during a run**

During one run, we recorded the detector signal at the start and then once per minute. The figure pairs the detector setup with the five readings: 1.10, 2.80, 5.20, 6.90 and 9.00 mV at 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 min, respectively. How can we predict the signal at 2.5 min, between two recorded times? A model describes signal as a function of time. We can evaluate it inside the measured interval (interpolation) or outside it (extrapolation). The dashed extension in the figure is an extrapolation beyond the last reading. Adding a model raises the next question: how do we choose a line that fits the measured points?

[[ref:ex:l8-script-material-1-1]]

**Estimate a model from measurements**

To describe the measured trend with a straight line, we estimate two numbers using all five time–signal pairs. The intercept gives the modelled signal at zero minutes in mV. The slope gives the modelled change in signal per minute in mV/min. The schematic shows how the measurements inform both coefficients. In the interactive plot, you can change each one and see what happens to the line.

[[ref:ex:l8-script-material-estimate-line]]

**Fit by eye: two coefficients**

Try different candidate lines for the same measurements. Change the intercept to raise or lower the line; change the slope to alter its tilt in mV per minute. The manual experiment starts at intercept 0 mV and slope 2.5 mV/min. As you move the sliders, compare the vertical gaps in the scatter plot with the residual bars. A point above the line appears above zero in the residual plot, and a point below the line appears below zero. Ask learners to improve the line and explain which vertical gaps their changes reduce. Do not reveal the fitted coefficient values yet. Compare the visible candidate curve with the fixed observation points; later the normal equations provide a reproducible solution.

[[ref:ex:l8-script-material-1-2]]

[[ref:ex:l8-script-material-1-3]]

**Give every vertical gap a sign**

Use the adjustable candidate line in [[ref:ex:l8-script-material-1-2]] to connect the scatter plot with the residual bars. Compute each observation minus its prediction at exactly the same time. A point above the line has positive residual; one below has negative residual. Move the sliders and check how the signed residuals change. These are vertical signal gaps, not perpendicular geometric distances.

**What happens when we add the signed gaps?**

Adding the five residuals gives 0.00 mV. Each point still misses the fitted line: positive and negative gaps cancel. The next step is to define a score that counts gaps on both sides.
**What should we minimise to fit a line?**

The comparison figure uses the same five measurements for two candidate lines. The starting line has intercept 0 mV and slope 2.5 mV/min, with residuals +1.10, +0.30, +0.20, −0.60 and −1.00 mV. The other line has intercept 1 mV and slope 2 mV/min, with residuals +0.10, −0.20, +0.20, −0.10 and 0.00 mV. Both signed sums are zero. Squaring the residuals before adding gives 2.70 mV² for the first line and 0.10 mV² for the second. A gap twice as large contributes four times as much. Absolute deviations would also prevent cancellation. The squared score is differentiable in the coefficients, which is useful when we derive the normal equations.

[[ref:ex:l8-script-material-1-7]]

[[ref:ex:l8-script-material-1-8]]

**Where is the squared error smallest?**

With the observations fixed, try changing one coefficient at a time. Each local error plot shows a slice of the squared-error surface near the corresponding slider setting. The other coefficient is held at its current value. Both plots mark the same current squared error. The total differential gives the first-order change in squared error for a change in both coefficients. At the joint minimum it is zero for every direction. We can vary one coefficient while keeping the other fixed. Doing this for each coefficient shows that both partial derivatives must be zero at the same pair of values. For these data, the quadratic curves upward and the pair is unique. To find the pair we need to solve the two equations together. Matrix notation gives us a compact way to do that.

[[ref:ex:l8-minimum-two-coefficients-script-1]]

**Matrix Algebra**

This short detour introduces the operations we will use to express the two regression conditions together.

**Matrix Shapes: count rows before columns**

Compare the 2 by 3, 3 by 2 and 2 by 4 arrays. Count horizontal rows first and vertical columns second. The first two arrays contain the same number of entries, but their shapes differ.

[[ref:ex:l8-script-material-2-2]]

**Matrix Indexing: row first, then column**

Read a subscript pair in a fixed order. In the shown matrix, a subscript 23 means row 2 then column 3, so its value is 6. It does not mean row 3 column 2, and it does not mean the number twenty-three. The box marks that matrix entry.

[[ref:ex:l8-script-material-2-4]]

**Matrix Types: square matrices**

Compare the 2 by 2, 3 by 3 and 4 by 4 examples. Every one is square because its row and column counts match. The positions and values of the entries can vary.

[[ref:ex:l8-script-material-2-6]]

**Matrix Types: diagonal matrices**

Compare diagonal matrices of sizes 2, 3 and 4. The highlighted diagonal is where the row and column indices agree. Every off-diagonal entry is zero. The 3 by 3 example has a zero on its main diagonal, which makes it singular.

[[ref:ex:l8-script-material-2-7]]

**Matrix Types: identity matrices**

Compare the identities of sizes 1, 2 and 3. Every diagonal entry is one. The left identity for a 2 by 3 matrix must have size 2, and the right identity must have size 3. Both products preserve the same matrix A.

[[ref:ex:l8-script-material-2-8]]

**Matrix Arithmetic: addition and subtraction**

Both matrices have the same shape. Read the top-left cells first: add 1 and 5 or subtract 5 from 1. Then do the same at each of the other three positions. The result keeps the original shape. When entries have units, the two values being combined must have compatible units.

[[ref:ex:l8-script-material-2-9]]

**Matrix Arithmetic: multiplication by a scalar**

Multiply each entry by the same scalar. The first calculation multiplies 1 by 2, and the remaining cells repeat the same operation with 2, 3 and 4. The positions and the shape stay the same. A dimensionless scalar preserves the units of the entries.

[[ref:ex:l8-script-material-2-10]]

**Matrix Transpose: rows become columns**

The first row [1,2,3] becomes the first column and the second row [4,5,6] becomes the second column. Shape two-by-three therefore becomes three-by-two. Transposing twice returns the original matrix. Later X transpose will collect dot products with the columns of X.

[[ref:ex:l8-script-material-2-11]]

**Matrix Multiplication: which dimensions must match?**

A matrix with m rows and n columns can multiply one with n rows and p columns. Each output entry needs a complete row and a complete column of equal length. The result has m rows and p columns. As a quick question, a two-by-three times a three-by-four is valid and yields two-by-four; the reverse order is not valid. Pause for the shape answer before continuing.

[[ref:ex:l8-script-material-2-12]]

**Matrix Multiplication: one row meets one column**

Each row of A has three entries and each column of B has three entries. Start with the boxed row and column. Multiply the three matching pairs and add to get 5 in the top-left cell. The other three cells use the three remaining row-column pairs and give 13, 14 and 31. The result has two rows from A and two columns from B.

[[ref:ex:l8-script-material-2-14]]

**Matrix Multiplication: sum the squares of a column**

Transpose the n by 1 column so that it becomes one row. Multiplying that row by the original column pairs each entry with itself and adds the products. For entries 2, 3 and 4 the result is 4 plus 9 plus 16, which is 29.

[[ref:ex:l8-column-squares-script]]

**Matrix Multiplication: why order matters**

Use a new pair of two-by-two matrices so both products have the same dimensions. The order still matters: AB and BA have different entries. Noncommutativity is about the operation, not a rounding error. For rectangular matrices one order may not even exist. Do not rearrange matrix factors as though they were scalar numbers.

[[ref:ex:l8-script-material-2-16]]

**Matrix Transpose: three useful rules**

Subtraction is entrywise, so swapping rows and columns preserves the difference between matching entries. For a product, the row of A and column of B become a column of A transpose and a row of B transpose. Their dot product is preserved by reversing the factors. Transposing a second time swaps the rows and columns back.

[[ref:ex:l8-transpose-rules-script]]

**Matrix Arithmetic: entrywise multiplication**

Hadamard multiplication combines corresponding entries of equally shaped matrices. For the same A and B it gives rows [5,12] and [21,32]. This is neither AB nor BA. In R, an asterisk is entrywise multiplication and percent-star-percent is matrix multiplication. Keep that distinction when reading model code.

[[ref:ex:l8-script-material-2-17]]

**Matrix Inverse: undoing a matrix product**

For the new example A = [[2,1],[1,1]], the inverse is [[1,−1],[−1,2]]. Check either multiplication order: the diagonal products sum to one and off-diagonal products sum to zero. An inverse is not obtained by taking reciprocals of individual entries. The inverse exists only for nonsingular square matrices.

[[ref:ex:l8-script-material-2-19]]

**Matrix Equations: write two equations as one**

The equations 2u1 + u2 = 5 and u1 + u2 = 3 become Au = b with the same inverse example and b = [5,3]. Left-multiply by the inverse to obtain u = [2,1]. Substitute back: 2 times 2 plus 1 equals 5 and 2 plus 1 equals 3. Row equations and the matrix equation describe the same problem.

[[ref:ex:l8-script-material-2-22]]

**Evaluate a line at five points**

Use the known intercept 2 and slope 0.5. Read the times in the order shown on the slide. Work through the first input 10, then build the whole matrix. The first column of ones carries the intercept into every row and the second column contains the five inputs. Each row times the same coefficient column yields one calculated response. Finally name the three objects X, b and y.

**Back to the Least-Squares Minimum**

Return from matrix algebra to the five detector readings. We can now use matrix operations to find the coefficients that minimise the squared error.

**Recall the total differential**

In [[ref:ex:l8-minimum-two-coefficients-script-2]], \(Q\) is the squared error and \(\mathrm dQ\) describes its first-order change as the coefficients vary. At the minimum, \(\mathrm dQ\) vanishes in every coefficient direction. Start with the term inside the square brackets, the residual of one observation.

**Put the residuals into a column**

The five-point example [[ref:ex:l8-five-point-matrix-script]] shows how a row of the design matrix times the coefficient column gives one prediction. Here \(\beta\) denotes that same coefficient column. In [[ref:ex:l8-script-material-4-2]], subtract the predicted column \(X\beta\) from the observed column \(y\). This gives the residual column \(e\).

**Write squared error as a matrix product**

Apply the squared-column rule in [[ref:ex:l8-column-squares-script]] to the residual column. In [[ref:ex:l8-script-material-4-5]], replace both copies of \(e\) by \(y-X\beta\). The transpose rules in [[ref:ex:l8-transpose-rules-script]] preserve the minus sign and reverse the factors in \((X\beta)^\top\).

**Expand the squared error**

Distribute the brackets of [[ref:ex:l8-script-material-4-5]] to get the four products in [[ref:ex:l8-expand-squared-error-script]]. Keep the order of the factors. Apply the product transpose rule in [[ref:ex:l8-transpose-rules-script]] to \(y^\top X\beta\). Reversing the factors gives \(\beta^\top X^\top y\). The whole product is a scalar, so its transpose is equal to its original value. This is why the two mixed terms combine in the final line.

**Differentiate term by term**

In [[ref:ex:l8-script-material-4-6]], differentiate the expanded squared error in [[ref:ex:l8-expand-squared-error-script]] while keeping \(X\) and \(y\) fixed. The constant contributes zero. The mixed term contributes a fixed vector.

**Differentiate the quadratic term**

In [[ref:ex:l8-quadratic-gradient-script]], the product rule differentiates each of the two occurrences of \(\beta\) once. Because \(X^\top X\) is symmetric, the two resulting vector contributions are identical. Their sum is \(2X^\top X\beta\).

**Solve the normal equation**

Set the gradient from [[ref:ex:l8-quadratic-gradient-script]] to zero. In [[ref:ex:l8-script-material-2-23]], divide by two and move \(X^\top y\) to the right.

**Isolate the coefficients**

In [[ref:ex:l8-isolate-coefficients-script]], multiply both sides from the left by \((X^\top X)^{-1}\), which exists when the design columns are independent. On the left, the adjacent factors are the inverse followed by its matrix. Their product is the identity, and \(I\widehat\beta=\widehat\beta\).

**The coefficient formula**

The result in [[ref:ex:l8-main-ols-formula-script]] gives the fitted coefficients from \(X\) and \(y\). To use it, first choose the columns of \(X\).

sections.body:
**Design matrix: intercept and linear term**

Read one row as b₀ + b₁xᵢ. For all five inputs, the equations stack into Xb. The first column is x⁰ = 1, including the intercept entry at x = 0. The second column is x itself. The design and its curve appear together in [[ref:ex:l8-basis-linear-script]].

**Design matrix: intercept and squared term**

Keep the constant column and square every input in the second column. This column multiplies b₂. There is no b₁ term. The parabola has its vertex at x = 0; only its right side is shown. The design and its curve appear together in [[ref:ex:l8-basis-square-script]].

**Design matrix: intercept, x and x²**

Keep both transformed columns. The x term tilts the parabola and shifts its vertex. Higher powers x³ and x⁴ are further columns if the model calls for them. The design and its curve appear together in [[ref:ex:l8-basis-quadratic-script]].

**Design matrix: combine sinh and cosh**

Use dimensionless x. The sinh column changes sign across zero, while cosh has the same value at x and minus x. Their weights are independent. These are hyperbolic functions; a reciprocal term is a different way to obtain a hyperbola. The design and its curve appear together in [[ref:ex:l8-basis-hyperbolic-script]].

**Design matrix: exponential column**

Exponentiate each dimensionless input before fitting. The multiplier of exp(x) is a coefficient. If an unknown coefficient were placed inside the exponential, the model would no longer be linear in that coefficient. The design and its curve appear together in [[ref:ex:l8-basis-exp-script]].

**Design matrix: logarithmic column**

Use positive, dimensionless inputs. The logarithm acts on x, while the response remains on its original scale. This differs from fitting a logarithm of the measured response. The design and its curve appear together in [[ref:ex:l8-basis-log-script]].

**Design matrix: reciprocal column**

Use nonzero x. Here the five inputs are positive and the curve tends toward the intercept. The reciprocal is undefined at zero, so never draw a continuous curve through zero. The design and its curve appear together in [[ref:ex:l8-basis-reciprocal-script]].

**Design matrix: square-root column**

For real-valued square roots, x must be nonnegative. This case uses the same five positive inputs as the exponential, logarithm and reciprocal examples. The transform is fixed before fitting. The design and its curve appear together in [[ref:ex:l8-basis-sqrt-script]].

**Design matrix: mix several functions**

The first five rows and a curve for chosen weights appear in [[ref:ex:l8-basis-mixed-script]]. The coefficient vector is (4, −0.15, 1.5, −1.2, 1.1, −2, 0.9) in the same order as the columns. Each additional fixed function comes with its own weight. The five displayed rows alone cannot identify all seven weights.

**How many columns can we fit?**

Read [[ref:ex:l8-basis-column-limit-script]] with \(p\) counting all estimated coefficients, including the intercept. A unique ordinary least-squares solution requires independent columns, which implies \(p\leq n\). With \(p=n\) and full rank, the fit interpolates the data and leaves zero residual degrees of freedom. If we want at least one residual degree of freedom, use \(p\leq n-1\). This count is necessary; we still need to check column independence.

**Design matrix: eight rows for seven coefficients**

In [[ref:ex:l8-basis-eight-rows-script]], add three input rows at 1.5, 2.5 and 3.5 to the five-row design. At full precision, the seven columns are independent. Given eight observed responses, the coefficient fit is unique and the residual degrees of freedom are \(8-7=1\). The curve uses the same chosen weights as the previous illustration.

**When is a model linear in its coefficients?**

The comparisons in [[ref:ex:l8-fixed-basis-coefficients-script]] use the same design-matrix rule: a term of the form \(b_j f_j(x)\) contributes the fixed column \(f_j(x)\). In \(\sinh(xb_4)\) and \(\exp(xb_2)\), the unknown changes the column itself, so fitting the original coefficient requires nonlinear regression. In \(\exp(x+b_2)\), factor out \(\exp(b_2)\) and fit \(u\) as the new linear coefficient multiplying the known column \(\exp(x)\). A real \(b_2=\ln(u)\) can only be recovered for \(u>0\). If an unconstrained fit gives \(u\leq 0\), it does not correspond to the original model.

**Five inputs, three design columns**

The matrix and model curve appear together in [[ref:ex:l8-gram-design-script]]. Use the five input values 1, 4, 9, 16 and 25. The columns are the constant one, x itself and the square root of x. The plotted curve is Xb at those inputs and the same model evaluated between them, using chosen coefficients.

**From one squared length to XᵀX**

Apply the column-product rule from [[ref:ex:l8-column-squares-script]] to each pair in [[ref:ex:l8-gram-rule-script]]. Recall that e transpose e is one dot product of a column with itself. X transpose X applies that rule to every pair of columns. A diagonal entry sums squares of one column. An off-diagonal entry sums products of two different columns in matching rows.

**Calculate XᵀX for the five inputs**

Use the design and curve in [[ref:ex:l8-gram-design-script]] as context for the matrix calculation in [[ref:ex:l8-gram-worked-script]]. Read the second column as x and the third as square roots. Multiply matching entries and sum. To get the second diagonal entry, square every x and add. To get entry row two, column three, multiply x by its square root in each row and add. Its mirror entry has the same value. Repeat with the column of ones and the third column to complete the matrix.

**Calculate Xᵀy from the measured responses**

In [[ref:ex:l8-xty-worked-script]], use the same design as in [[ref:ex:l8-gram-design-script]] and add a column of measured responses. Keep the same five input rows and align the example measurements 2, 3, 5, 6 and 9 with them in order. Multiply each design column entry by the matching measured response and add the five products. The constant column gives the response sum, the x column gives 380, and the square-root column gives 92. This is the right-hand side of the normal equation.

**The coefficient formula: what is still missing?**

See [[ref:ex:l8-inverse-remaining-script]]. We already have both products. Call X transpose X G and X transpose y r. The inverse notation describes the solution. We can get the same coefficients by solving G beta hat equals r directly. Refer back to [[ref:ex:l8-gram-worked-script]] for \(X^\top X\) and [[ref:ex:l8-xty-worked-script]] for \(X^\top y\). If the columns of \(X\) are independent, \(G\) is invertible and the formula may also be written as \(\widehat\beta=G^{-1}X^\top y\).

**Two ways to handle the inverse**

For an invertible two-by-two matrix, use the determinant formula. For a symmetric positive-definite matrix, use Cholesky factorisation. Cholesky factors can be used to form the inverse or solve the normal equations directly. Use the references to read more about each method. See the comparison in [[ref:ex:l8-inverse-methods-script]]. Further reading: [[ref:ex:l8-inverse-methods-determinant-script]] and [[ref:ex:l8-inverse-methods-cholesky-script]].

sections.body:
**Build the drift design and response**

Starting from the five readings in [[ref:ex:l8-script-material-1-1]], [[ref:ex:l8-drift-products-script]] lists the rows of \(X\) and \(y\) together. Pair the intercept column with itself to count five observations. Its product with the time column is \(0+1+2+3+4=10\), and the time column with itself gives \(0^2+1^2+2^2+3^2+4^2=30\). These fill \(X^\top X\). For \(X^\top y\), the intercept pairs with the readings to give their sum, 25 mV. The time column weights those readings by 0 through 4 min, giving 69.9 min·mV.

**Back to the detector: fit the drift line**

Substitute the products from [[ref:ex:l8-drift-products-script]] in [[ref:ex:l8-drift-fit-script]]. The determinant is \(5\cdot30-10^2=50\). Multiplying the inverse by \(X^\top y\) gives an intercept of 1.02 mV and a slope of 1.99 mV/min.

**Back to the detector: predict the signal at 2.5 min**

Return to the five detector readings from [[ref:ex:l8-script-material-1-1]]. The least-squares line shown in [[ref:ex:l8-drift-prediction-script]] is \(\widehat y=1.02+1.99t\), with \(t\) in minutes and \(\widehat y\) in millivolts. Evaluating it at 2.5 min gives \(1.02+1.99\cdot2.5=5.995\) mV. The requested time falls between two observed times, so this is interpolation.

**A heating ramp with a changing rate**

The temperature was recorded once a minute for four minutes. The least-squares straight line in [[ref:ex:l8-heating-straight-check-script]] assumes a constant change per minute. Its residuals are positive at both ends and negative in the middle. That systematic pattern suggests that the temperature rises faster later in the run.

**Add a column for squared time**

In [[ref:ex:l8-heating-quadratic-fit-script]], each row pairs one observation with three known inputs. The intercept column contains ones. The next column contains elapsed time \(x\) in minutes, and the third contains its square \(x^2\) in minutes squared. At 3 min, for example, the inputs are 1, 3 and 9, and the observed response is 29.66 °C. The same ordinary least-squares procedure estimates three coefficients. The fitted coefficients are 21.00 °C for the intercept, 0.50 °C/min for time and 0.80 °C/min² for squared time. The sum of squared residuals falls from 8.964 °C² for the line to 0.004 °C² for the quadratic fit on these observations.

**An exponential decay on two scales**

[[ref:ex:l8-log-decay-observations-script]] starts with five tracer concentrations in mg/L. The first one-minute drop is about 5.65 mg/L, while the last is only about 1.67 mg/L. If a similar fraction of the tracer remains after each minute, the same relative loss translates into a smaller absolute drop as the concentration declines.

The transformation in [[ref:ex:l8-log-decay-transform-script]] divides each positive measured concentration by the reference of 1 mg/L before taking its natural logarithm. Time stays in minutes. The difference between two consecutive logarithms is the logarithm of the ratio of their concentrations. A constant retention fraction therefore produces an equal step for each equal time interval.

In [[ref:ex:l8-log-decay-fit-script]], both panels show the same observations. The line in [[ref:ex:l8-log-decay-line-formula-script]] is fitted by ordinary least squares on the log scale, with an intercept of about 2.996 and a slope of −0.40 per minute. Apply the exponential in the second equation to the fitted log values to recover a curve in mg/L. Each minute the model retains about 67% of the preceding concentration. The regression minimises squared errors on the log scale.

**Multiple linear regression with two measured predictors**

[[ref:ex:l8-multiple-regression-design-script]] shows six synthetic detector readings for three concentrations at two temperatures. Each row pairs both settings with one response. The design columns contain ones, the measured concentration, and the measured temperature in °C. As in earlier examples, ordinary least squares estimates all coefficients at once.

[[ref:ex:l8-multiple-regression-products-script]] starts from the same six rows. Apply [[ref:ex:l8-multiple-regression-products-formula-script]] by multiplying entries in corresponding rows and adding the products. For example, pairing concentration with temperature gives \((20+30)(1+2+3)=300\). This value appears in both symmetric positions of \(X^\top X\). For \(X^\top y\), the ones sum the six signals to 33, the concentrations weight them to give 74, and the measured temperatures weight them to give 840.

In [[ref:ex:l8-multiple-regression-coefficients-script]], substitute the two products in the coefficient formula. Multiplying by the inverse yields −1.00 mV for the intercept, 2.00 mV per mg/L for the concentration slope, and 0.10 mV per °C for the temperature slope. The intercept is the model prediction at zero concentration and 0 °C, outside the measured settings.

In [[ref:ex:l8-multiple-regression-plane-script]], the fitted signal forms a plane above the two predictor axes. Fixing temperature at 20 or 30 °C cuts that plane along a straight line. Both cuts have the same concentration slope because the model uses a single concentration coefficient. The six dots are the measured signals at the corresponding concentration and temperature.

[[ref:ex:l8-multiple-regression-fit-script]] plots the fitted signal against concentration at two fixed temperatures. The coefficient of concentration measures the change in fitted signal per mg/L while temperature stays fixed. The temperature coefficient measures the change per degree while concentration stays fixed. In [[ref:ex:l8-multiple-regression-fit-formula-script]], this works out to 2 mV per mg/L and 1 mV per 10 °C. The fitted profiles are parallel because the model assigns a common concentration slope to both temperatures. The next example uses the same regression with 0/1 predictors for a categorical variable.

sections.body:
**One-way ANOVA as a linear regression**

The river-water SPE example from Level 7 has eighteen independent preparations, six per method. In [[ref:ex:l8-anova-recovery-design-script]], the response column contains the original recoveries. The design matrix has a column of ones and two 0/1 indicators, for methods B and C. Method A is the reference because both indicators are zero for its rows. An additional indicator for A would make the columns dependent, since the three indicators sum to the intercept column.

In [[ref:ex:l8-anova-recovery-products-script]], the design rows are grouped by method and each pattern occurs six times. The products in [[ref:ex:l8-anova-recovery-products-formula-script]] show why the intercept counts 18, B and C each count six, and their overlap is zero. Multiplying by the observed responses sums 1710 across all preparations and selects the method totals 588 for B and 558 for C.

[[ref:ex:l8-anova-recovery-coefficients-script]] applies the inverse to those sums. Its first row takes the total minus the B and C sums, leaving 564 for method A. Dividing by six gives 94% recovery. The other two rows give the differences from A, +4 and −1 percentage points.

[[ref:ex:l8-anova-recovery-fit-script]] compares two ordinary least-squares models. The intercept-only model predicts the grand mean (95%) for every sample. The model with method predicts the mean of each group (94%, 98%, 93%). With A as the reference, the fitted intercept is 94% and the two adjustments are +4 and −1 percentage points. The null hypothesis of equal group means is the joint hypothesis that both adjustments are zero.

In [[ref:ex:l8-anova-recovery-formula-script]], the drop in residual sum of squares from 114 to 30 is the between-method sum of squares, 84. The group model adds two coefficients and leaves fifteen residual degrees of freedom. Substitution in [[ref:ex:l8-anova-recovery-formula-script]] gives \(F=(84/2)/(30/15)=21\), the same statistic as one-way ANOVA. This comparison uses the classical ANOVA assumptions when interpreting the F test.
